stem: How is the **feed conversion ratio (FCR)** of a farm animal calculated?

options.content: Gain in body mass ÷ mass of feed eaten
options.rationale: This gives the efficiency (as a fraction), not the FCR.

options.content: Mass of feed eaten ÷ gain in body mass
options.rationale: A lower FCR means less feed per kilogram of gain.

options.content: Mass of feed eaten × gain in body mass
options.rationale: Multiplying the two has no meaning here.

options.content: Final body mass ÷ starting body mass
options.rationale: This ignores the feed eaten.

explanation: FCR = mass of feed eaten ÷ gain in body mass. For example, 4 kg of feed for 2 kg of gain gives an FCR of 2. A lower FCR means better conversion.
hints: The FCR tells you how many kilograms of feed are needed for each kilogram of gain.

stem: What type of pathogen causes foot-and-mouth disease in cattle?

options.content: A bacterium
options.rationale: Anthrax is caused by a bacterium.

options.content: A flatworm
options.rationale: Liver fluke is a flatworm.

options.content: A protoctist
options.rationale: Redwater is caused by a protoctist.

options.content: A virus
options.rationale: Foot-and-mouth disease is caused by a highly infectious virus.

explanation: Foot-and-mouth disease is caused by a virus. It spreads very easily, so it is controlled by vaccination, quarantine and movement control; antibiotics do not work against it.
hints: Antibiotics cannot cure this disease.

stem: True or false: a lower feed conversion ratio means that an animal converts its feed into body mass more efficiently.

answerSpec.feedbackTrue: Correct. A lower FCR means less feed is needed for each kilogram of gain.
answerSpec.feedbackFalse: It is true. FCR is feed ÷ gain, so a lower value means less feed for each kilogram gained.

explanation: FCR = mass of feed eaten ÷ gain in body mass. The lower the FCR, the less feed is needed for each kilogram of gain, so the conversion is more efficient.
hints: The feed goes on the top of the fraction.

stem: How is redwater spread from one cow to another?

options.content: By ticks
options.rationale: Ticks carry the protoctist from animal to animal.

options.content: By water snails
options.rationale: Snails are part of the liver fluke life cycle.

options.content: By spores in the soil
options.rationale: That is how anthrax spreads.

options.content: By drinking dirty water
options.rationale: Redwater is not spread through water.

explanation: Redwater is caused by a protoctist that lives in red blood cells. Ticks carry it from animal to animal, so dipping to kill ticks is the main control.
hints: Dipping controls this disease.

stem: Name the type of organism that causes anthrax.

rejected.feedback: Foot-and-mouth disease is caused by a virus; anthrax is caused by a bacterium.
Redwater is caused by a protoctist.

explanation: Anthrax is caused by a bacterium (Bacillus anthracis) that forms spores. The spores can survive in soil for many years.
hints: It forms spores that last for years in the soil.

stem: A pig ate 240 kg of feed and gained 80 kg in body mass. Calculate its feed conversion ratio.
explanation: $\text{FCR} = \dfrac{240}{80} = 3.0$. The pig needed 3 kg of feed for each kilogram of body mass gained.
workedSolution:
1. $\text{FCR} = \dfrac{\text{mass of feed eaten}}{\text{gain in body mass}}$.
2. $\dfrac{240}{80} = 3.0$.
hints: Divide the feed eaten by the gain in mass.

stem: A broiler chicken ate 3.2 kg of feed and gained 1.8 kg. Calculate its food conversion efficiency as a percentage, to one decimal place.
explanation: Efficiency $= \dfrac{1.8}{3.2} \times 100 = 56.25 \approx 56.3\%$.
workedSolution:
1. Efficiency $= \dfrac{\text{gain in body mass}}{\text{mass of feed eaten}} \times 100$.
2. $\dfrac{1.8}{3.2} \times 100 = 56.25\%$, or $56.3\%$ to one decimal place.
hints: Efficiency puts the gain on top and multiplies by 100.

stem: Cattle grazing on veld have a much higher feed conversion ratio than broiler chickens kept in a warm house. Which is the best explanation?

options.content: Cattle do not respire, so they waste food.
options.rationale: All animals respire.

options.content: Grass contains no energy.
options.rationale: Grass contains energy, but much of it is hard to digest.

options.content: Much of the grass is lost undigested, and grazing cattle use energy walking and keeping warm.
options.rationale: Cellulose passes out in the faeces, and walking and keeping warm use energy, so less of the feed becomes body mass.

options.content: Broilers are larger than cattle, so they need less food for each kilogram of growth.
options.rationale: Broilers are much smaller than cattle.

explanation: Grass is high in cellulose, much of which passes out undigested in the faeces. Grazing cattle also walk long distances and release a lot of energy as heat. Broilers eat concentrated, easily digested feed, move little and are kept warm, so more of their feed becomes body mass.
hints: Think about where the energy in the feed ends up.

stem: Match each livestock disease with the type of organism that causes it.
explanation: Anthrax: bacterium. Foot-and-mouth disease: virus. Liver fluke: parasitic flatworm. Redwater: protoctist spread by ticks. None of the four is caused by a fungus.
hints: One type of organism is not used.

stem: A cow dies suddenly with dark blood oozing from its nose and mouth, and a veterinary officer suspects anthrax. What should be done with the carcass?

options.content: Cut it up quickly so the meat can be sold before it spoils
options.rationale: The meat could infect people, and opening the carcass spreads the disease.

options.content: Leave it unopened and burn it or bury it deeply, away from water
options.rationale: Opening the carcass lets the bacteria form spores that survive for years.

options.content: Leave it in the field for vultures to clean up
options.rationale: Scavengers open the carcass and spread spores.

options.content: Treat it with antibiotics and then eat the meat
options.rationale: Meat from an animal with anthrax must never be eaten.

explanation: When an anthrax carcass is opened, the bacteria are exposed to air and form tough spores that can survive in the soil for many years. The carcass must be left unopened and burned or buried deeply, and the meat must never be eaten because anthrax can infect people.
hints: What do the bacteria form when exposed to air?

stem: A farmer near Masvingo grazes his sheep on wet, marshy land beside a dam, and many have liver fluke. Which plan would best control the problem?

options.content: Dip the sheep every week to kill ticks
options.rationale: Dipping controls ticks, not liver fluke.

options.content: Give the sheep antibiotics in their drinking water from the dam
options.rationale: Antibiotics kill bacteria, not flatworms.

options.content: Vaccinate the sheep against anthrax and dip them to kill ticks
options.rationale: This does not affect liver fluke.

options.content: Dose the sheep with a flukicide and drain the marshy land where the snails live
options.rationale: This kills the flukes and breaks the life cycle; fencing off the marsh also works.

explanation: Dosing (drenching) kills the flukes inside the animals. Fencing off or draining wet areas keeps the animals away from the water snails and the cysts on wet grass, breaking the life cycle.
hints: Which animal does the liver fluke need to complete its life cycle?

stem: There is an outbreak of foot-and-mouth disease in a district. Which measures are used to control it?

options.content: Quarantine, controlling the movement of cattle, and vaccination
options.rationale: These stop the virus spreading to new herds.

options.content: Treating every animal in the district with antibiotics
options.rationale: Antibiotics do not work against viruses.

options.content: Dipping cattle every week to kill the ticks that spread it
options.rationale: Foot-and-mouth disease is not spread by ticks.

options.content: Draining marshy land to kill snails
options.rationale: Snails are involved in liver fluke, not foot-and-mouth disease.

explanation: Foot-and-mouth disease is caused by a highly infectious virus. Outbreaks are controlled by quarantine, banning the movement of animals and animal products without permits, vaccination, and keeping cattle away from buffalo, which can carry the virus.
hints: The disease is caused by a virus and spreads easily between animals.

stem: Complete the sentences about redwater.

payload.template: Redwater is caused by a {{blank:cause}} that destroys red blood cells. It is carried from cow to cow by {{blank:vec}}. Farmers control it mainly by {{blank:ctrl}} their cattle.

explanation: Redwater is caused by a protoctist in the red blood cells, spread by ticks and controlled by dipping or spraying cattle to kill the ticks.
hints: Dip tanks are used against this disease.

stem: Name the animal in which the larvae of the liver fluke must develop before they can infect cattle or sheep.

rejected.feedback: Ticks spread redwater, not liver fluke.
Mosquitoes spread malaria, not liver fluke.
Cattle are the main host; the larvae develop first in another animal.

explanation: Liver fluke eggs pass out in dung and hatch in water. The larvae enter a water snail and develop inside it, then leave and form cysts on wet grass, which cattle and sheep eat.
hints: It lives in wet, marshy places and in water.

stem: Why is the urine of a cow with redwater red or brown?

options.content: The cow has been drinking muddy water.
options.rationale: This is not the reason.

options.content: The ticks inject red dye into the blood.
options.rationale: Ticks carry the parasite; they do not inject dye.

options.content: Red blood cells are destroyed, and their haemoglobin passes into the urine.
options.rationale: This is how the disease got its name.

options.content: The kidneys are making extra red blood cells that leak into the urine.
options.rationale: Kidneys do not make red blood cells.

explanation: The redwater parasite lives in red blood cells and destroys them. Haemoglobin released from the burst cells is carried to the kidneys and passes into the urine, colouring it red or brown. The cow also becomes anaemic.
hints: What red pigment do red blood cells contain?

stem:
A small-scale farmer in Marondera compared two feeds for broilers. Each bird was weighed at the start and end of the trial.

| Feed | Mean feed eaten per bird / kg | Mean gain in mass per bird / kg | Cost of feed per kg / US\$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| A | 4.2 | 2.4 | 0.70 |
| B | 4.5 | 2.25 | 0.55 |

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Calculate the feed conversion ratio for feed A.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Calculate the feed conversion ratio for feed B.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Which feed did the birds convert into body mass more efficiently?

options.content: Feed A
options.rationale: Feed A has the lower FCR (1.75).

options.content: Feed B
options.rationale: Feed B has the higher FCR (2.0), so more feed was needed per kilogram of gain.

options.content: Both equally
options.rationale: The FCRs are different.

options.content: It cannot be told from the data
options.rationale: The FCRs can be calculated from the data.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Calculate the cost of feed A needed for each kilogram of gain, in US\$.

parts.label: (e)
parts.stem: Calculate the cost of feed B needed for each kilogram of gain, in US\$.

parts.label: (f)
parts.stem: Which feed should the farmer choose? Give **two** reasons, using the data.

points.description: Feed B, because it costs less per kilogram of gain (US\$1.10 against about US\$1.23)
Even though feed A converts more efficiently (FCR 1.75 against 2.0) / other factors, e.g. time to reach market mass, more trials or more birds needed before deciding

parts.explanation: Feed B is the better choice on cost: it costs about US\$1.10 per kilogram of gain compared with about US\$1.23 for feed A, even though feed A is converted more efficiently (FCR 1.75 against 2.0). Because feed A gives faster gain, birds might reach selling mass sooner, so the farmer should also consider time and repeat the trial with more birds.

explanation: FCR A $= \dfrac{4.2}{2.4} = 1.75$; FCR B $= \dfrac{4.5}{2.25} = 2.0$, so A is converted more efficiently. Cost per kg of gain: for A, $1.75 \times 0.70 = 1.225$, so US\$1.225 (about US\$1.23); for B, $2.0 \times 0.55 = 1.10$, so US\$1.10. Feed B is cheaper per kilogram gained despite its higher FCR.
workedSolution:
1. (a) $\dfrac{4.2}{2.4} = 1.75$.
2. (b) $\dfrac{4.5}{2.25} = 2.0$.
3. (d) Cost per kg of gain $=$ FCR $\times$ price per kg of feed $= 1.75 \times 0.70 = 1.225$, about US\$1.23.
4. (e) $2.0 \times 0.55 = 1.10$, so US\$1.10.
hints: FCR = feed ÷ gain.
Cost of feed per kg of gain = FCR × cost of 1 kg of feed.

stem: Before a communal dipping programme started, the 400 cattle using one dip tank carried a mean of 85 ticks per animal and there were 28 cases of redwater in a year. After a year of regular dipping, the mean was 12 ticks per animal and there were 5 cases.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Calculate the percentage decrease in the mean number of ticks per animal. Give your answer to one decimal place.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Calculate the percentage of the 400 cattle that had redwater in the year **before** the programme.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Explain why dipping reduced the number of cases of redwater.

points.description: Dipping kills ticks (with an acaricide / chemical)
Ticks are the vectors that carry the redwater protoctist, so fewer ticks means fewer cattle infected

parts.explanation: The dip chemical kills ticks. Ticks are the vectors that carry the redwater parasite between cattle, so with fewer ticks, fewer cattle were infected.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Suggest **two** ways in which fewer cases of redwater would improve the productivity of the herd.

points.description: Fewer deaths
Faster growth / less weight loss / more milk / better fertility / stronger oxen for ploughing / lower costs of treatment

parts.explanation: Fewer cattle would die, and healthy cattle grow faster, give more milk, breed better and are strong enough to plough, while the farmers spend less on drugs.

explanation: Tick decrease $= \dfrac{85 - 12}{85} \times 100 = 85.9\%$. Before the programme $\dfrac{28}{400} \times 100 = 7\%$ of the cattle had redwater (afterwards $\dfrac{5}{400} \times 100 = 1.25\%$). Dipping kills the ticks that carry the protoctist, so fewer cattle are infected and the herd is more productive.
hints: Percentage decrease = decrease ÷ original value × 100.
What carries the redwater parasite?

stem: Explain why only a small proportion of the feed eaten by a beef cow becomes body mass. [5]

points.description: Some of the feed is not digested (e.g. cellulose in grass) and is lost in the faeces
Some is excreted, e.g. nitrogen from excess amino acids lost as urea in urine
Much of the energy is released in respiration
and used for movement (walking to graze and drink), breathing and other life processes
and lost as heat / used to keep body temperature constant
Some parts of the body (bones, hide) are not useful as meat

answerSpec.modelAnswer: Much of the grass a cow eats is cellulose, which is hard to digest, so a large part of the feed passes out undigested in the faeces. Some of the absorbed nutrients are excreted; for example, excess amino acids are turned into urea, which leaves in the urine. Most of the energy that is absorbed is released in respiration and used for movement, such as walking to grazing and water, and for breathing, digestion and other life processes. Much of this energy ends up as heat, and the cow uses energy to keep its body temperature constant. Only the remainder is used for growth, so only a small proportion of the feed becomes body mass, and some of that (bones and hide) is not eaten as meat.

explanation: Feed is lost in faeces and urine, and most of the absorbed energy is used in respiration for movement and life processes and lost as heat, leaving little for growth.
hints: Follow the feed: what is not digested, what is excreted, and what is respired.

stem: Describe the cause, spread and effects of foot-and-mouth disease and how it is controlled, and explain why an outbreak can harm a whole country's economy. [6]

points.description: Caused by a virus (highly infectious)
Spread by contact between animals, contaminated vehicles, boots or animal products, the air / carried by African buffalo
Effects: fever, blisters on mouth, feet and teats, lameness, less eating, weight loss, lower milk yield
Control: quarantine and movement control / permits
Control: vaccination; separating cattle from buffalo (fences); disinfecting; antibiotics do not work
Economy: bans on moving or selling cattle and on exporting beef; lost income for farmers and the country
Economy: costs of vaccination and control; lost draught power for ploughing and lower crop production

answerSpec.modelAnswer: Foot-and-mouth disease is caused by a highly infectious virus that affects cloven-hoofed animals such as cattle, goats and pigs. It spreads by direct contact between animals, on contaminated vehicles, boots and animal products, and through the air, and African buffalo can carry it. Infected cattle develop a fever and blisters on the mouth, tongue, feet and teats; they drool, go lame, eat less, lose weight and give less milk. Because antibiotics do not work against viruses, outbreaks are controlled by quarantine, strict controls on moving animals and animal products, vaccination, keeping cattle away from buffalo and disinfecting vehicles. An outbreak can harm the whole economy because cattle and beef cannot be moved, sold or exported from affected areas, farmers lose income, and the costs of vaccination and control are high; sick oxen also cannot plough, so crop production may fall.

explanation: A full answer gives the cause (virus), spread, effects on the animals, control measures, and the economic effects of movement and export bans.
hints: Cover cause, spread, effects, control and the economy in turn.

stem: Which practice would most improve the productivity of a herd of dairy cows?

options.content: Letting the cows walk long distances to graze each day
options.rationale: Long walks use energy that could have produced milk.

options.content: Feeding a balanced ration and vaccinating the cows against disease
options.rationale: Good nutrition and health increase milk yield.

options.content: Keeping more cows than the pasture can support
options.rationale: Overstocking leaves each cow short of food.

options.content: Giving the cows less water so they eat more
options.rationale: Cows need plenty of water to make milk.

explanation: Productivity rises when animals get a balanced diet (with protein for milk and growth) and plenty of water, stay healthy, and do not waste energy walking long distances. Overstocking and water shortage reduce yield.
hints: What do cows need to produce a lot of milk?

stem: How do cattle usually become infected with liver fluke?

options.content: By being bitten by ticks that have fed on infected cattle
options.rationale: Ticks spread redwater.

options.content: By breathing in spores from the soil while grazing
options.rationale: This is how anthrax can be caught.

options.content: Through direct contact with the blisters or saliva of an infected cow
options.rationale: This is how foot-and-mouth disease spreads.

options.content: By eating wet grass on which fluke larvae from snails have formed cysts
options.rationale: Grazing near water is the main risk.

explanation: Larvae leave the water snails and form cysts on wet grass near water. Cattle and sheep swallow the cysts while grazing; the young flukes then travel to the liver.
hints: The larvae develop in an animal that lives in wet places.

stem: A farmer in Chivi keeps 20 cattle that graze near a wetland. He dosed 10 of them against liver fluke and left the other 10 undosed. Over six months the mean gain in mass was 48 kg for the dosed cattle and 30 kg for the undosed cattle. Dosing cost US\$2 per animal, and the cattle sell for US\$2.50 per kilogram of live mass.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Calculate the extra gain in mass of a dosed animal compared with an undosed animal.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Calculate the extra profit from dosing one animal, after paying for the dose.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Explain why the undosed cattle gained less mass.

points.description: Flukes damage the liver (and cause anaemia)
so less of the feed is converted into body mass / energy is used fighting the infection / the cattle eat less

parts.explanation: Liver flukes damage the liver and cause anaemia, so the cattle convert less of their food into body mass; sick animals also tend to eat less.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Suggest **two** further measures the farmer could take to reduce liver fluke on his farm.

points.description: Fence off or drain the wetland
Control the water snails / graze on drier pasture / dose all the cattle regularly

parts.explanation: He could fence off or drain the wet grazing near the wetland, control the water snails, move the cattle to drier pasture and dose all of them regularly.

parts.label: (e)
parts.stem: Suggest why the farmer should repeat the trial before deciding that dosing is always worthwhile.

points.description: Only 10 animals in each group / the groups may have differed in other ways (age, breed, grazing) / one season only

parts.explanation: Each group had only 10 animals, so chance differences in age, breed or grazing could affect the result; repeating the trial would show whether the result is reliable.

explanation: Extra gain $= 48 - 30 = 18$ kg, worth $18 \times 2.50 = 45$, so the extra profit is $45 - 2 = 43$, that is US\$43 per animal. Flukes damage the liver, so infected cattle convert feed less efficiently. Draining or fencing wetland and controlling snails break the fluke's life cycle.
workedSolution:
1. (a) $48 - 30 = 18$ kg.
2. (b) Value of the extra gain $= 18 \times 2.50 = 45$, so US\$45.
3. Extra profit $= 45 - 2 = 43$, so US\$43 per animal.
hints: Find the extra mass first, then its value, then subtract the cost of the dose.
Which animal must be present for the fluke's life cycle to continue?
